title: Google's Gemini 2.5 Flash introduces 'thinking budgets' that cut AI costs by 600% when turned down
summary: Google has launched Gemini 2.5 Flash with a new feature called "thinking budgets" that lets users dial model compute and reasoning intensity. Google says lowering these budgets can sharply reduce inference costs — with reductions described as up to 600% in some scenarios — while preserving acceptable output for cost-sensitive tasks. The feature targets developers and enterprises looking to balance accuracy, latency and price.
content:
Google today announced Gemini 2.5 Flash, an incremental update to its Gemini family of large models that adds a configurable "thinking budgets" control aimed at reducing inference costs for commercial users.

According to Google, thinking budgets let developers set how much internal compute and multi-step reasoning the model is allowed to use for a given query. Turning budgets up prioritizes deeper, more resource-intensive reasoning; turning them down reduces internal deliberation and compute usage to deliver answers with lower latency and cost.

In marketing materials and technical notes, Google suggests that reducing the thinking budget can lead to dramatic cost reductions in many real-world workloads. The company uses the phrase "cut AI costs by 600% when turned down" to convey the scale of savings in some benchmarked scenarios, though actual results will depend on task complexity, prompt design and acceptable accuracy trade-offs.

Experts caution that such percentage figures can be interpreted in different ways: a 600 percent figure is often shorthand for a multi-fold reduction in cost rather than a literal algebraic decrease. Google emphasizes that thinking budgets are intended as a practical lever for teams that run high-volume inference pipelines and are willing to trade some degree of depth in reasoning for much lower operational expenses.

The feature integrates with Google Cloud endpoints and the Gemini API, allowing enterprises to apply thinking budgets per model, per endpoint or even per request. Google also released guidance on profiling workloads to identify areas where reduced reasoning produces acceptable outcomes and where it does not.

Industry watchers say thinking budgets mirror growing attention across the AI ecosystem on cost-efficiency tools, such as early-exit networks, model quantization, routing and mixed-precision strategies. By exposing a simple control, Google hopes to make cost/quality trade-offs accessible to teams without deep model engineering expertise.

Privacy and safety remain important considerations. Google notes that lower thinking budgets can change the model's behavior and encourages testing, safety checks and monitoring before rolling changes into production. The company also plans to collect anonymized telemetry to refine default settings and recommended profiles.

For many businesses, even modest per-request savings compound quickly across millions of queries. Whether the new control will change enterprise buying patterns or push competitors to offer similar budget-style knobs remains to be seen, but the feature underscores a broader shift: as models improve, operators are increasingly focused on tunable efficiency as well as raw capability.
